paras: The threatened lynching of John Carter took place in October 1888 at Mayfield, Kentucky, where a crowd cried "lynch him" during the examining trial of Carter, a butcher's son accused of murdering the horse trader William Trafford. Officers removed Carter to the jail at Paducah, which was heavily guarded against an expected mob, and no attack on him was reported.

According to a Louisville dispatch dated October 6, Harriet Hurd, described as "an old colored woman," had found Trafford's remains in the woods near Mayfield the day before. Trafford's head had been crushed as if by a heavy stick and his throat cut, and a Kentucky roundup added that hogs had eaten part of the body. An inquest was held, and suspicion fell on Carter, who had been in Trafford's company the night before at "a house of ill repute."
Officers went after Carter, whom the Kentucky papers described as a boy of 17, and found him at Cold Water, twelve miles from Mayfield.

At Carter's examining trial, the woman testified that he had gone out with Trafford and returned alone, saying Trafford "had more money than sense," and blood stains were reported on Carter's clothes. While the hearing was in progress a crowd gathered, and cries of "lynch him" were heard. The officers got Carter away "with difficulty" and lodged him in jail at Paducah. That night the jail was heavily guarded because a mob was still expected, and a Portland brief two days later said Carter was under guard "to prevent his being lynched."
The coverage does not report an attack on the jail, nor any indictment or trial of Carter for Trafford's death.

The fullest account was the Louisville dispatch printed by the Savannah Morning News on October 7 under the headlines "Lynchers Cry for His Life" and "A Horse Trader Murdered by His Companions in a Debauch." The dispatch reported the crowd's cries without comment and gave the evidence against Carter as testimony from the examining trial.

Northern papers reduced the story to a sentence or two among general news: the Portland Daily Press kept the lynching threat on October 8, while the Vermont Watchman on October 10 mentioned only the discovery and the suspicion against Carter. Kentucky weeklies, the Big Sandy News and the Hickman Courier, ran an identical paragraph in a state news column in mid-October that dwelt on the condition of the body and said nothing of the crowd. None of the papers gave the race of Carter or Trafford.

The finder's surname appears as Hurd in the Louisville dispatch and as Curd in the Vermont and Kentucky papers. The dispatch, dated Saturday, October 6, placed the discovery on the previous day, while the Vermont Watchman said the body was found on Saturday.

reader.title: Threatened lynching of John Carter
bases: A crowd cried 'lynch him' at the examining trial of a murder suspect and a mob was expected at the jail, a threatened lynching in which no one was killed (A1, A2).
Carter was not killed; officers removed him to the Paducah jail, which was guarded against an expected mob (A1, A2). The crowd's threat was tied to the murder accusation, but no killing occurred.

The murder and Carter's arrest are reported in differently worded accounts (A1, A3, A4), but the lynching threat rests on the Louisville dispatch (A1) and a two-line brief probably condensed from it (A2); the Kentucky roundup (A4, A5) does not mention a mob.

accounts.label: Louisville dispatch
accounts.gist: Trafford's body was found, an inquest held, and Carter arrested at Cold Water; during the examining trial a crowd cried 'lynch him,' officers got Carter to the Paducah jail, and a mob was still expected that night.

accounts.label: Kentucky state roundup
accounts.gist: Describes the mutilated body and Carter's arrest at Coldwater, giving his age as 17, without mentioning a crowd or lynching threat.

framing.detail: The Savannah Morning News ran the dispatch under 'Lynchers Cry for His Life,' reporting the crowd's cries without comment and the evidence against Carter as testimony.
Northern papers carried one- or two-sentence briefs among general news; the Portland Daily Press kept the lynching threat, the Vermont Watchman did not.
The Kentucky roundup 'The Commonwealth' stressed the gruesome details ('hogs had devoured part of the body') and omitted the crowd.

info: Trafford's body was found on Friday, October 5, 1888, by the Louisville dispatch's 'yesterday' (dated Oct. 6); the Vermont Watchman says Saturday. The examining trial and the crowd's cries came after Carter's arrest, before the night of October 6.
Mayfield, Ky. (body found in the woods near or in the suburbs of Mayfield); Carter taken to the jail at Paducah
John Carter, son of a Mayfield butcher, aged 17 in the Kentucky roundup; race not stated

Suspected of murdering William Trafford, a horse trader, whose head was crushed and throat cut; testimony at the examining trial said Carter had gone out with Trafford and returned alone, and that his clothes had blood stains
